section.title: Feature-Level Specification
section.description:
- For every feature listed in Section 6.1, provide a detailed design using the same Fx ID and feature name. - Each subsection must match the feature ID, name, and priority defined in Section 6.1. - No additional features beyond those in Section 6.1 may be specified here.
- SCOPE — this section captures REPRODUCIBLE REQUIREMENTS, not implementation decisions: - WRITE here (the WHAT, reproducibly): what each user action must do, which layers it crosses (UI → API → data), what must be true for it to be correct (acceptance criteria, edge cases, error responses the user sees). - DO NOT write here (the WHY/HOW — these belong to an ADR or to the code): why a particular library / algorithm / key design was chosen, alternatives considered, trade-offs, tuning constants, exact column lists, or framework-specific snippets. - Rule of thumb: if a sentence would still be true after the team swaps the database or the hashing library, it belongs here. If it justifies *that choice*, it belongs in an ADR. - Each feature here becomes one ADR category via `/feature-to-adr`. The PRD states the requirement once; the ADR then owns the architectural decision and the code owns the implementation. Keep this section free of decisions so the ADR is not a duplicate.

template.title: Feature Template
template.header: Feature ID: Fx | Priority: Must-Have / Should-Have / Nice-to-Have

subsection.title: User Story
subsection.description: - Describe the user scenario for implementing this feature. - Use this format: As a [persona], I want to [action], so that [benefit].
subsection.example: - As a new user, I want to sign up with my email, so that I can access the service.

subsection.title: User Flow
subsection.description: - Describe the user flow for this feature. - Keep the flow simple and concise.
subsection.example: 1. Display a sign-up form with: - Email input field - Password input field - "Sign Up" button 2. When the user submits the form: - Validate input - Trigger an API call - Redirect to the main screen upon successful sign-up

subsection.title: Technical Description
subsection.description: - Describe the implementation as a vertical slice: trace each user action end-to-end from UI through API to data store, so this feature can be developed and tested independently. - For each key action in the user flow, describe WHAT happens at each layer it touches (UI / API / data) — at the level of behavior and responsibility, not implementation. - Stay reproducible, stay decision-free: - DO state: the action, the layers it crosses, the data it reads/writes (conceptually), what is returned to the user, and any shared interface this feature relies on (e.g., "uses the shared auth session", "writes to the user record"). - DO NOT state: chosen libraries/algorithms (e.g., bcrypt, JWT), exact column lists, tuning constants, or why one approach was picked over another — those are architectural decisions (→ ADR) or implementation details (→ code), and pinning them here makes the PRD churn whenever the code does. - Keep API references at the endpoint level (method + path + purpose); leave request/response schemas to the code. - If this feature shares resources with other features (e.g., a common table or auth middleware), note the shared interface rather than redefining it.
subsection.example: 1. Submit Sign-up Form - UI: Sign-up form sends the email and password to the sign-up endpoint (POST /api/auth/signup) - API: validates the input, rejects duplicates, and creates the user with the password stored in non-recoverable (hashed) form - Data: a new user record is persisted - Response: the user is authenticated and lands on the main screen 2. Validate Email (real-time) - UI: as the user leaves the email field, checks availability (GET /api/auth/check-email) - API: looks up whether the email is already taken - Response: an inline message tells the user if the email is available > (How the password is hashed, the auth token format, and the user table's columns are architectural/implementation choices — leave them to the ADR and the code, not this section.)

subsection.title: Edge Cases
subsection.description: List potential edge cases and how they should be handled.
subsection.example: - User submits an already registered email → Show "Email already exists" error - User enters a password with less than 8 characters → Show validation error - Network timeout during API call → Show retry option

subsection.title: Error Handling
subsection.description: Define error scenarios and appropriate responses.
subsection.example: | Error Type | HTTP Code | User Message | |------------|-----------|--------------| | Validation failure | 400 | "Please check your input" | | Duplicate email | 409 | "Email already registered" | | Server error | 500 | "Something went wrong. Please try again." |

subsection.title: Acceptance Criteria
subsection.description: - Define the conditions that must be met for this feature to be considered complete. - Use clear, testable statements.
subsection.example: - [ ] User can enter email and password in the sign-up form - [ ] Form validates email format before submission - [ ] Password must be at least 8 characters with one special character - [ ] Successful sign-up redirects user to main screen - [ ] Duplicate email shows appropriate error message - [ ] All error states display user-friendly messages
